title: Jail death followed drinking binge: inquest
article: A coroner's inquest into the case of a New Brunswick man who died in police custody in 2007 heard Monday that the man had been on a three-week drinking binge.
Randy Nelson Trenholm, 50, of Port Elgin, had been arrested for impaired driving by the District 4 RCMP on June 1 and taken to the lockup in Shediac.
He later had difficulty breathing and collapsed. Police said they performed cardiopulmonary resuscitation, but Trenholm was pronounced dead at the Dr. Georges-L.-Dumont Hospital the next day.
His family has been seeking answers ever since.
Coroner John Evans told the four-man, one-woman jury in Moncton that Trenholm was an alcoholic who had been on a three-week binge when he was arrested.
On June 2, about 6 a.m., a jail guard noticed Trenholm was agitated and starting to shake, so an ambulance was called, but paramedics said Trenholm's vitals were fine and left, the jury heard.
At 8:42 a.m., the guard noticed Trenholm on the floor shaking and the ambulance was called again. Police started CPR, but Trenholm was in cardiac arrest and declared dead at the hospital.
The inquest also heard that the video monitoring system in the jail failed to record images that night.
But Staff Sgt. Daniel Copp, of the Fredericton police, who investigated Trenholm's death, said he sent the machine for evaluation to a company in Ontario and there was no evidence of tampering.
Trenholm had stopped at a store in Port Elgin the evening of June 1 to buy beer, the jury was told. A friend at the store noticed Trenholm appeared intoxicated and offered to drive him home.

An RCMP cruiser was in the store's parking lot and pulled the car over shortly after it left. Although Trenholm's friend was behind the wheel, Trenholm was still arrested for impaired driving for having driven to the store.
A week has been set aside for the inquest.
"The jury will hear evidence from witnesses under subpoena in order to determine the facts of the death," said Greg Forestell, the province's chief coroner.
"The presiding coroner [John Evans] is responsible to ensure the jury maintains the goal of fact-finding not fault-finding," he said.
Trenholm's family members are upset with the way the case has been handled and have hired their own lawyer to find out what happened.

Forestell said he hopes this process brings answers - "not only [for] the family, but the general public as well to fully ascertain what all the facts are surrounding the death and really just to ensure that no death goes unnoticed by the community."
The inquest may come up with recommendations aimed at preventing similar deaths.
